2

What is the long-run return to learning more in primary school?

What we already know

More years of schooling are associated with higher earnings.

≈ 10% per year
A very large corpus of researchMore than 50 years of work, spanning hundreds of studies and many countries.
The missing causal evidence

Does improving literacy and numeracy in primary school change adult outcomes?

Before this study, no causal estimates of these long-run returns in low- and middle-income countries—and very limited evidence in high-income settings.
3

In 2003, we began the LEAPS study in rural Punjab, Pakistan.

Pakistan

 

Punjab

Within Punjab, the study covered three districts.

4

We began in 2003 and returned repeatedly through 2018.

2003

The study begins

Baseline school and household surveys across 112 rural villages. Children take tests in mathematics, Urdu and English.

2004–07

Repeated school surveys

Researchers return in successive years, following cohorts and measuring changes in learning across schools.

2011–12

Another follow-up

Return to the villages to test children again and update information on schooling and families.

2018–19

Adult survey

Track the original cohort across Pakistan and beyond—then measure skills, education, employment and earnings.

Survey rounds and longitudinal tracking: Andrabi et al. (2026), LEAPS research design and data collection timeline.

6

Two complementary strategies to study long-run effects of foundational learning

Explore how two different shocks that improve primary school test scores affect the same children's outcomes as adults.

Route 1

Attend a 1 sd higher value-added school

Use differences in primary-school quality generated by switches across primary schools.

Annual primary test score increase: +0.19 sd
Route 2

Attend a school in a village assigned report cards

Use a randomized information intervention that improved learning across the village.

Primary test score increase 1 year later: +0.11 sd
Then we estimate the long-run effects on adult test scores, education, employment, and earnings.
Source: Andrabi et al. (2026)
7

Approach #1: Children who start out in same school switch to different schools

7–8 schoolsTypically available within the local schooling market

LEAPS village satellite image.
8

Approach #2: Randomly provide report cards to villages

Control village

Schools and families continue without report cards.

Treatment village

Families receive school and child test-score information.
The intervention raised test scores by 0.11 standard deviations—at a direct cost of about $3 per student in 2003.
Illustration uses the same supplied Punjab village image in both panels; treatment assignment was at village level. Andrabi et al. (2017, 2026).

12

The benefits were not confined to boys or to the rich.

Women

Higher primary-school quality increases educational attainment for girls as well as boys.

Evidence on women’s earnings is less precise, in a setting where paid work is uncommon.

Suggestive evidence that female employment increases (+57%)—but on a low base.

Education gains are broadly similar.

Poorer children

Children from low-SES households also benefit from better foundational learning.

Estimated earnings gains for low-SES children are similar to, or larger than, those for high-SES children at this stage of life.

The benefits do not accrue only to the rich.
Andrabi et al. (2026), heterogeneity by socioeconomic status and gender.

15

Should we think bigger when investing in learning?

A 1 sd better primary school raises adult test scores by 0.19 sd.
The implied lifetime earnings gain is about $1,650 per student.
For a school with 106 students, that is about $175,000 in benefits.
After all estimated social costs: about $99,000 in net benefits.
≈ $1,000in additional expenditure per child could be justified for this improvement in quality
Low-cost interventions are not the only investments worth trying.
Andrabi et al. (2026), conclusion. The $1,000 figure refers to a 1 sd improvement in school value-added sustained across the primary-school years.
